node.label: Kathleen M. Brown
node.date_label: “Brave New Worlds” 1993 · “Changed … into the Fashion of Man” 1995 (collected 1997) · Good Wives 1996 · Foul Bodies 2009 · Undoing Slavery 2023
node.description: In Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996), Brown argues that gender hierarchy helped create racial categories and slavery in colonial Virginia, while racial slavery transformed gender relations. Household labor, sexuality and the differing legal treatment of English and African women help explain the consolidation of white male authority. Janet L. Coryell praised the book as “a marvelous synthesis,” noting only, as “a truly minor quibble,” that Brown does not particularly examine the intellectual underpinnings of notions about gender or race. Brown’s own retrospective on Edmund S. Morgan acknowledges his inspiration while asking how white women helped reproduce racism. Foul Bodies (2009) extends the inquiry to cleanliness and the domestic work behind public ideals of civilization; Janet Moore Lindman reads it as connecting bodily care, gender and empire.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Brave New Worlds: Women’s and Gender History” (1993); “Changed … into the Fashion of Man” (1995; collected in The Devil’s Lane, 1997); Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs: Gender, Race, and Power in Colonial Virginia (1996); Foul Bodies: Cleanliness in Early America (2009; paperback 2011); Undoing Slavery: Bodies, Race, and Rights in the Age of Abolition (2023; paperback 2026).
node.scope_note: Complete 2001 retrospective, 2014 original interview and Coryell review read. Book arguments are read through publisher descriptions, displayed openings and named reviewers; none of Brown’s monographs was read in full. Only the displayed Lindman and Sharon Block review extracts were read. The 1993, 1995 and 1998 article bodies remain unread. Laboring Women was not read on a permitted route.

proposed_edges.relationship: Brown identifies Morgan’s American Slavery, American Freedom (1975) as an inspiration for Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) in “Americans on the James” (2001).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Brown’s own 2001 retrospective, opening paragraph: “the copy that inspired my first book.” Full essay read; Morgan’s book unread. This explicit debt is distinct from Brown’s criticism of its explanation.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Americans on the James” (2001), Brown argues that Morgan’s American Slavery, American Freedom (1975) leaves white women’s investment in reproducing racism insufficiently explained.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2001 essay, paragraphs beginning But Morgan’s ambitious effort and The stake of white women. Brown preserves Morgan’s explanatory ambition while supplementing his political-strategy account. Full essay read; original Morgan book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: White women and the reproduction of racism

proposed_edges.relationship: Reflecting on Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) in the 2014 Junto interview, Brown recalls developing the project while enrolled in the Women’s History Program under Gerda Lerner’s guidance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: First answer, paragraph 1: “under the guidance of Gerda Lerner.” Original interview read; no specific Lerner work or formal dissertation-supervisor relationship is asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Lerner’s guidance in the Women’s History Program

proposed_edges.relationship: Brown (series co-editor from 2002, as Brown's own CV records) and Daniel K. Richter co-edit the Early American Studies book series published by the University of Pennsylvania Press with the McNeil Center for Early American Studies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher front-matter PDF p. 2 (unnumbered series page): “Series Editors”; p. 4 gives copyright 2004. A formal joint editorial credit, not shared employment; no claim of coauthorship or volume editing, founding date, or continuous tenure. Undirected collaboration uses comparison metadata.
proposed_edges.map_label: Joint editors of Early American Studies

proposed_edges.relationship: Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) makes changing gender relations and ideals of masculinity part of the explanation of racial slavery and colonial authority.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UNC description, paragraphs 1–4; corroborated by Coryell pp. 1–2 and Brown’s 2014 answer on teaching. Publisher and complete review read; original book unread. This is a specific analytical contribution, not a claim to have founded gender history.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender in the making of colonial power

proposed_edges.relationship: Brown retrospectively describes Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) as an effort to show race, gender and class becoming mutually constitutive through historical processes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 2014 interview, second answer: Brown describes race, gender and class as “socially constructed and mutually constitutive” and says she had yet to read history treating “intersectionality as a truly historical process.” Interview read; no claim that Brown coined the term or derived the book from a named intersectionality theorist.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foul Bodies: Cleanliness in Early America (2009) connects changing ideas of health and bodily care to domestic labor, gender and public standards of civilization, as Janet Moore Lindman explains in her 2010 review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lindman’s publisher-displayed extract, first two paragraphs, citing Brown p. 3; Yale description also read. Rest of review and book body unread. The edge is mediated by this named scholarly reading and limited to health, bodily care and their social organization.

proposed_edges.relationship: In an American Historical Review review (June 1999) of Gordon-Reed's Thomas Jefferson and Sally Hemings: An American Controversy (1997), Brown calls the book a 'persuasive critique of the consensus view among Jefferson scholars' and writes that it strengthened Brown's own inclination to believe that the Jefferson-Hemings relationship occurred.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's own first-page preview (Oxford Academic, AHR 104.3, June 1999, p. 900, right column). Reviewer metadata on the landing page: Kathleen M. Brown, University of Pennsylvania. Phrases seen: 'Annette Gordon-Reed's persuasive critique of the consensus view among Jefferson scholars that there was no sexual relationship has strengthened my inclination toward belief'; 'Through careful research and meticulous reasoning, the virtuosity of which cannot be fairly represented in a short review, she argues that the evidence dismissed as insufficient by dozens of historians amounts to a strong circumstantial case'; 'The case being tried by Gordon-Reed is concerned less with Jefferson's sexual behavior, however, than with the intellectual integrity of a group of prominent Jefferson scholars, including Dumas Malone and Merrill Peterson'. Limits: pp. 901-902 (the rest of the review, including any reservations) unread; the claim is limited to the first page. A favourable review that reports being persuaded on one question is recorded as comparison, not as a broader intellectual debt. The review is also listed in Brown's own CV (book reviews section). Gordon-Reed is a run member, so the endpoint is pending.
proposed_edges.map_label: Brown reviews Gordon-Reed on Jefferson and Hemings

proposed_edges.relationship: In Laboring Women (2004), Jennifer L. Morgan identifies Brown’s Good Wives, Nasty Wenches, and Anxious Patriarchs (1996) as a precedent for subsequent early American histories and explicitly engages Brown’s argument about women’s role in naturalizing slave status through race.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed Google Books search-preview excerpts, not the complete introduction or chapter. The p. 5 excerpt names Brown’s 1996 book and assesses its importance for later histories. On p. 93 Morgan explicitly attributes to Kathleen Brown an argument about women naturalizing slave status through race. The latter is substantive engagement in the body of Morgan’s argument, not an acknowledgment or isolated bibliographic citation. The complete surrounding pages and endnotes remain unread; no exclusive intellectual derivation is claimed. Penn’s own record confirms the original 2004 publication, distinct from the 2011 ebook date.
proposed_edges.map_label: Morgan engages Brown on gender and slave status

proposed_edges.relationship: Brown’s “Changed ... into the Fashion of Man”: The Politics of Sexual Difference in a Seventeenth-Century Anglo-American Settlement (1995) contributes to histories of sex ambiguity by interpreting community sex classification and the colonial labor interests surrounding the Thomas/ine Hall case, arguments that Maayan Sudai examines in “Sex Ambiguity in Early Modern Common Law” (2021; journal issue 2022).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the open publisher PDF’s introduction, pp. 478–481; the Hall discussion, pp. 486–487; and the Brown reference on p. 509. On p. 487 Sudai specifically attributes the labor explanation to Brown (1995, 188–190), then contrasts Brown’s account of unstable sex differences with Norton’s interpretation. This is sustained body-text engagement. The field edge concerns historical sex classification, matching the existing queer node’s scope of changing sexual categories; it does not assign a modern identity to Hall or claim Brown invented the field. Brown’s original article and the rest of Sudai’s article were not read. Sudai is not an eligible person endpoint, so no person node or personal edge is proposed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Sex ambiguity, community judgment and colonial labor
